issues.legal_issue: A State law on a concurrent subject ceases to operate when an applicable Central law contains repugnant provisions on that subject.
material_facts: The State law and the Central law both governed land acquisition, a subject in the Concurrent List.
The Central law became applicable in the State and its provisions were substantially different from those of the State law.
The parties accepted that the State law stood repealed when the Central law became applicable.
issues.conclusion: The State law stood repealed by operation of Article 254 when the repugnant Central law became applicable; no express provision repealing the State law was necessary.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 254 of the Constitution, repugnancy between an applicable Central law and a State law on a concurrent subject results in the State law being displaced. That consequence operates automatically and may arise by necessary implication; the Court relied on Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors. [1959] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 8.

predicates.concurrent_subject_law: The State law and the Central law both regulate a subject on which both legislatures may make laws.
predicates.central_law_applies: The Central law has become applicable to the territory governed by the State law.
predicates.provisions_conflict: The applicable Central law contains provisions repugnant to provisions of the State law on the same subject.

issues.definition: When both laws regulate a concurrent subject, the Central law applies, and their provisions conflict, the State law ceases to operate.

issues.legal_issue: Valid steps already taken in a pending acquisition proceeding under a repealed State law remain effective, and the proceeding may continue from the stage it had reached under the applicable Central law.
material_facts: Acquisition proceedings began under the State law, and a preliminary notification and declaration were issued under it.
A challenge to the declaration was dismissed, and the declaration had been upheld by the High Court.
When the Central law became applicable and the State law was repealed, further acquisition proceedings remained pending.
The acquisition officer later issued notice to make an award without issuing a fresh preliminary notification under the Central law.
issues.conclusion: The valid steps taken under the State law up to the declaration were not effaced by repeal, and the acquisition officer could continue the pending proceeding from the stage it had reached without beginning the procedure afresh.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6(b) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 provides that repeal does not affect the previous operation of the repealed enactment or anything duly done under it, unless a different intention appears. The Court relied on Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors. [1959] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 8, which recognized that duly completed steps under a repealed enactment are preserved.

rule.if: acquisition_proceeding and proceeding_pending and central_law_applies and state_law_steps_valid

predicates.acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding is for the acquisition of land.
predicates.proceeding_pending: The proceeding had not reached completion when the replacement law became applicable.
predicates.central_law_applies: A Central law governing the acquisition became applicable while the proceeding was pending.
predicates.state_law_steps_valid: Steps already taken under the State law were legally valid and had not been set aside.

issues.definition: A pending acquisition proceeding may continue from its existing stage when valid steps were taken under the former State law before the applicable Central law replaced it.
